metadata.title: Claude, Dsar Response.
metadata.purpose: Answer what it actually takes to answer a data subject access request: not just checking the one system where the person is an obvious record, but searching every system under every identifier they've used, then sending back only their data. Lands the carry-out that the response is only complete once every system is searched under every name and address, and what goes back is theirs alone.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks what data a company holds on them. The reflex is one lookup — the one database with their name in it. That's not what the request is asking. The real question is which systems, under which name.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What's in our database about them?', hesitates on 'database', corrects to 'systems', lands the real question

props.text:
What's in
our database
about them?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('database' -> 'systems') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Every company has one system that looks like the obvious place to check: the customer database. Ask it, and it answers loudly — record found. It feels complete because it was built to feel complete, optimized to give marketing one row per customer. That's a different job from giving legal every trace of a person — support tickets, mailing lists, an old account from an earlier CRM. A customer database was never built to see any of them.

shot.new_visual_element: A customer-record card, fully lit; three system chips (support tickets, mailing list, old account) slide past it, dim and disconnected, never touching it

production_viz.label: One system was never built to see the rest
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'CUSTOMER DATABASE' with a 'RECORD FOUND' stamp, fully lit. Three dim, unlit chips labelled 'support tickets', 'mailing list', 'old account' slide in from the side and pass underneath the record card without touching it. A caption fades in beneath: 'it can't see the rest.'

beats.narration_text: The procedure is the other way around. Not: check the obvious system. Instead: search every system that could hold a record, under every identifier the person has ever used. Follow one requester through those systems. The customer database has them under their current email — the identifier the signup form asked for. Support tickets carry them by name only, because the queue keys on whoever the agent typed in. The mailing list still has an account under an email they closed two years ago.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three cards revealing the same requester under three different identifiers

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- same person, three identifiers
production_viz.mechanic: Three cards left to right: 'DATABASE' showing 'CURRENT EMAIL', 'SUPPORT TICKETS' showing 'NAME ONLY', 'MAILING LIST' showing 'CLOSED EMAIL'. Each card in turn dims the one before it as it lands. THIS EXACT THREE-CARD CHAIN RETURNS, RESOLVED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Query only the current email, and the mailing-list record doesn't come back at all — it's filed under an address the mail server no longer recognizes. A complete file needs all three keys — name, both emails, ticket history — matched and merged. Two consequences flip the naive intuition. A system that returns zero hits under one identifier hasn't cleared the person; it's only cleared that one string. And a hit isn't automatically theirs to ship — a support ticket that names a coworker too has to be cut back to their information alone before it goes out.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- three cards collapse into one complete file, then split into two both-directions cautions

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- complete file, and what ships
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 THREE-CARD CHAIN RETURNS, identical placement, and collapses into one card reading 'COMPLETE FILE', highlighted terracotta -- the three identifiers listed beneath it. It then splits into two cards: left reads 'no hit on one identifier' beside a card labelled 'does not mean no data'; right reads 'a hit turns up' beside a card labelled 'redact the rest before it ships', with a coworker's name visibly struck out inside a small ticket mockup.

beats.narration_text: The response is complete on two conditions. Every system searched, under every identifier the person has ever used. And what goes back is their data — only their data.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I need to answer a Data Subject Access Request — someone has asked me to send them every piece of personal data my organization holds on them. Before I pull records, help me build a defensible search plan. Ask me to list every system where we might hold customer or user data. Ask me to list every identifier this person has ever used — every email, every name, every account ID, every phone, every address. Then produce a search matrix: for each system, which identifiers to try, in what order. Flag any system where a hit is likely to contain someone else's data too, so I know what needs redacting before it ships. Go deeper: ask the same model where a DSAR search plan usually breaks in practice — which systems get forgotten, which identifiers get skipped, which redactions get missed under time pressure. Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I need to answer a Data Subject Access Request — someone has asked me to send them every piece of personal data my organization holds on them. Before I pull records, help me build a defensible search plan. First, ask me to list every system where we might hold customer, employee, or user data. Then ask me to list every identifier this specific person has ever used with us — every email, every legal name and preferred name, every account ID, every phone number, every physical address. Then produce a search matrix: for each system, which identifiers to try, and in what order. Flag any system where a hit is likely to contain data that belongs to someone else too — support tickets, shared documents, email threads — so I know exactly which records need redacting before they leave the building.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: ask the same model where a DSAR search plan usually breaks in practice — which systems get forgotten, which identifiers get skipped, and which redactions get missed under time pressure — and what one process change would catch each of those failures earlier.
